topics.name: Algebra
topics.summary: Working with unknowns: expressions, equations and how to solve them.

topics.name: Fractions & Decimals
topics.summary: Converting between forms and calculating confidently with both.

objectives.text: Explain what a variable stands for in an expression.
Write a word problem as an algebraic expression.
Identify the terms and coefficients in an expression.

keyTerms.definition: A letter standing in for a number you do not know yet.
The number multiplying a variable. In 3x the coefficient is 3.
One piece of an expression, separated from the next by + or −.
A term with no variable, so its value never changes.
A collection of terms with no equals sign. It has a value, not a solution.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
Algebra begins when you stop needing to know a number in order to work with it.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

• say what a letter in an expression stands for
• name the terms and coefficients in an expression
• turn a sentence in words into an algebraic expression

sections.heading: What a variable is
sections.body:
A variable is a letter that stands in for a number you do not know yet. In the expression 3x + 5, the letter x is the variable. It has no fixed value — it waits for you to find out what it is. The number 3 in front of it is called the coefficient, and it means "three lots of x".

This is the idea that makes algebra useful. You can describe a situation, and do arithmetic on that description, before you know any of the numbers. The price of cassava can change every week; the rule "three bundles cost 3x" stays true whatever x turns out to be.

Notice that 3x is a multiplication with the sign left out. Algebra drops the × because it looks too much like the letter x.
sections.example: If a bundle of cassava costs x dollars, then 3 bundles cost 3x dollars. When x turns out to be 25, the three bundles cost 3 × 25 = 75 dollars.

sections.heading: Terms and coefficients
sections.body:
An expression is built from terms separated by plus or minus signs. In 4a + 7b − 2, there are three terms: 4a, 7b and −2. The coefficient of a is 4 and the coefficient of b is 7. The term −2 has no variable at all, so it is called a constant — its value never changes.

The sign belongs to the term that follows it. In 4a + 7b − 2 the third term is −2, not 2. Getting this right matters the moment you start moving terms around.

A letter written on its own has a coefficient of 1. In x + 5, the coefficient of x is 1, even though nothing is written in front of it.
sections.example:
In 9m − n + 6:

    terms        → 9m, −n, 6
    coefficients → 9 for m, −1 for n
    constant     → 6

sections.heading: Turning words into algebra
sections.body:
Most of algebra is translation. "Five more than a number" becomes n + 5. "Twice a number, less three" becomes 2n − 3. Read the sentence slowly and write down each piece in the order it appears, then check that your expression says the same thing as the words.

One warning about order. "Five more than a number" and "five less than a number" do not translate the same way round: the first is n + 5, but the second is n − 5, not 5 − n. Subtraction cares about order; addition does not.

The safest check is to invent a number. Pick n = 10 and read both the words and your expression. If they give different answers, the translation is wrong.
sections.example:
A taxi charges 40 dollars to start plus 15 dollars for each kilometre. The cost of a journey of k kilometres is 40 + 15k.

Check with k = 3: the words say 40 + three lots of 15 = 40 + 45 = 85. The expression gives 40 + 15 × 3 = 85. They agree.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
A market woman buys n crates of tomatoes at 250 dollars each. She also pays 600 dollars to transport the whole load. Write an expression for her total cost, then find the cost when she buys 7 crates.

Step 1 — name what is unknown.
    n is the number of crates.

Step 2 — write each cost as a term.
    crates: 250 each, n of them → 250n
    transport: a flat 600, however many crates → 600

Step 3 — combine.
    total cost = 250n + 600

The 250 is a coefficient because it multiplies the variable. The 600 is a constant because it does not change with n.

Step 4 — use it. For 7 crates, substitute n = 7:
    250 × 7 + 600 = 1750 + 600 = 2350 dollars.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body:
**Writing 3x when you mean 3 + x.** 3x means three lots of x. If the words say "three more than x", the expression is x + 3.

**Losing the sign in front of a term.** In 4a − 7b the second term is −7b. Students who record it as 7b get the right answer to the wrong question later on.

**Thinking x always means the same number.** x is whatever the problem makes it. In one question it is 5, in the next it is 200.

**Translating "five less than n" as 5 − n.** It is n − 5. Test it with a number: five less than 12 is 7, and 12 − 5 = 7, while 5 − 12 = −7.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. In 6y − 4, name the coefficient, the variable and the constant.

2. Write an expression for "eight more than twice a number p".

3. A phone costs 45 dollars plus 12 dollars per month. Write the cost after m months.

4. In 5a + b − 9, how many terms are there, and what is the coefficient of b?

5. Sia is x years old. Her brother is 4 years younger. Write his age, then check it with x = 15.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• A variable is a letter standing in for an unknown number.
• A coefficient is the number multiplying a variable; a letter alone has coefficient 1.
• Terms are separated by + and −, and the sign belongs to the term after it.
• A constant has no variable and never changes.
• To translate words, write the pieces in order, then test with a number you choose.

objectives.text: Check a solution by substituting it back.
Solve an equation with the variable on both sides.

keyTerms.definition: A statement that two expressions are equal. It has an equals sign and a solution.
The value of the variable that makes both sides equal.
The operation that undoes another: subtraction undoes addition, division undoes multiplication.
To put a number in place of a letter.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
An expression has a value. An equation has a solution. This lesson is about finding it.

By the end you will be able to:

• solve equations in one step and in two steps
• solve an equation where the letter appears on both sides
• check any answer for yourself, so you never have to wonder whether it is right

sections.heading: The balance rule
sections.body:
An equation says two things are equal. Picture a balance scale: whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other, or the scale tips. That single rule is the whole of equation solving. To get x by itself, undo whatever has been done to it — and do the same undoing on both sides.

Every operation has an inverse. Addition is undone by subtraction. Multiplication is undone by division. You are not moving numbers across the equals sign by magic; you are doing the same thing to both sides and letting one side simplify.
sections.example:
x + 7 = 12. Seven has been added to x, so subtract 7 from both sides:

    x + 7 − 7 = 12 − 7
    x = 5

sections.heading: Two-step equations
sections.body:
When x has been multiplied and then added to, undo in reverse order: deal with the addition or subtraction first, then the multiplication. This is the opposite of the order you would use to build the expression up.

Think of it as unwrapping a parcel. The last layer put on is the first layer taken off. In 3x + 4, the 4 was added last, so the 4 comes off first.
sections.example:
3x + 4 = 19.

    subtract 4 from both sides → 3x = 15
    divide both sides by 3     → x = 5

sections.heading: Variables on both sides
sections.body:
Sometimes the letter appears on both sides, as in 5x − 3 = 2x + 12. The balance rule still does all the work: collect the variable terms on one side and the numbers on the other.

Subtract the smaller variable term from both sides. Here 2x is smaller than 5x, so subtract 2x from each side. That removes x from the right entirely and leaves an ordinary two-step equation.

Choosing the smaller term keeps the coefficient positive, which is easier to work with and gives fewer sign errors.
sections.example:
5x − 3 = 2x + 12.

    subtract 2x from both sides → 3x − 3 = 12
    add 3 to both sides         → 3x = 15
    divide both sides by 3      → x = 5

Check: left 5 × 5 − 3 = 22. Right 2 × 5 + 12 = 22. They match.

sections.heading: Always check your answer
sections.body:
Substituting your answer back into the original equation costs ten seconds and catches almost every mistake. Put the number in place of the letter and work out both sides separately. If they match, you are right.

This is the part most students skip and the part that most reliably turns a lost mark into a gained one. You do not need the teacher, the answer sheet or anyone else: the equation itself tells you whether you are correct.
sections.example:
Check x = 5 in 3x + 4 = 19.

    Left side:  3 × 5 + 4 = 15 + 4 = 19
    Right side: 19

They match, so x = 5 is correct.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
Solve 4(x − 1) + 2x = 26 and check the answer.

Step 1 — expand the bracket.
    4x − 4 + 2x = 26

Step 2 — collect like terms on the left.
    6x − 4 = 26

Step 3 — undo the subtraction.
    add 4 to both sides → 6x = 30

Step 4 — undo the multiplication.
    divide both sides by 6 → x = 5

Step 5 — check in the ORIGINAL equation, not the tidied one. Checking in your own working would hide a mistake made in step 1.

    4(5 − 1) + 2 × 5 = 4 × 4 + 10 = 16 + 10 = 26 ✓

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body:
**Doing something to one side only.** 3x = 15 becomes x = 5, not x = 12. Divide both sides.

**Undoing in the wrong order.** In 3x + 4 = 19, dividing by 3 first gives x + 4/3, which is correct but far harder. Take the +4 off first.

**Checking in your own working.** Always substitute into the original equation. If you copied it down wrongly, only the original will reveal it.

**Sign errors with the variable on both sides.** Subtracting the larger variable term leaves a negative coefficient, which is legal but invites mistakes. Subtract the smaller one.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. x − 6 = 11

2. 5x = 40

3. 2x + 9 = 23

4. 7x − 5 = 3x + 15

5. Check your answer to question 4 by substituting it into both sides.

6. A number is doubled and then 7 is added, giving 31. Write the equation and solve it.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• An equation is a balance: do the same thing to both sides.
• Undo operations with their inverses, in reverse order.
• With the letter on both sides, subtract the smaller variable term first.
• Always substitute your answer back into the original equation.
• A checked answer needs no one else to confirm it.

objectives.text: Expand a bracket using the distributive law.
Solve an equation that contains brackets.

keyTerms.definition: The rule that a(b + c) = ab + ac: the outside number multiplies every term inside.
To remove a bracket by multiplying it out.
Terms with exactly the same variable part, which can be added together.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
Brackets group a whole expression so it can be multiplied in one go. Removing them correctly is the skill this lesson builds.

By the end you will be able to:

• expand a bracket using the distributive law
• handle a minus sign in front of a bracket without losing marks
• solve an equation that contains brackets

sections.heading: Expanding brackets
sections.body:
The number outside a bracket multiplies everything inside it — every term, not just the first. This is the distributive law. Missing the second term is the single most common slip in this topic, so write the multiplication out in full until it becomes automatic.

It helps to draw two arrows, one from the outside number to each term inside, and to say the multiplication aloud as you write it.

A minus sign outside the bracket belongs to the multiplier. In −3(x + 2), you are multiplying by −3, so BOTH terms change sign: −3x − 6.
sections.example:
4(x + 3) means 4 times x plus 4 times 3, which is 4x + 12. It does not mean 4x + 3.

And −3(x + 2) = −3x − 6, not −3x + 6.

sections.heading: Solving with brackets
sections.body:
Expand the bracket first, then solve the equation the ordinary way with the balance rule. Take care with a minus sign outside a bracket: it changes the sign of every term inside.

If the same variable appears more than once after expanding, collect the like terms before you start undoing. 2x + 3x is 5x; 2x + 3 is not 5x, because those are not like terms.
sections.example:
2(x − 5) = 14.

    expand              → 2x − 10 = 14
    add 10 to both sides → 2x = 24
    divide by 2          → x = 12

Check: 2(12 − 5) = 2 × 7 = 14 ✓

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
Solve 5(x + 2) − 3(x − 1) = 21.

Step 1 — expand the first bracket.
    5(x + 2) = 5x + 10

Step 2 — expand the second. The multiplier is −3, so both signs flip.
    −3(x − 1) = −3x + 3

That +3 is where most marks are lost. Minus times minus gives plus.

Step 3 — write the whole left side and collect like terms.
    5x + 10 − 3x + 3 = 21
    2x + 13 = 21

Step 4 — solve.
    subtract 13 → 2x = 8
    divide by 2 → x = 4

Step 5 — check in the original.
    5(4 + 2) − 3(4 − 1) = 5 × 6 − 3 × 3 = 30 − 9 = 21 ✓

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body:
**Multiplying only the first term.** 4(x + 3) is 4x + 12, never 4x + 3. Arrows to both terms.

**Forgetting the sign flip.** −3(x − 1) is −3x + 3. A minus outside changes every sign inside.

**Adding unlike terms.** 2x + 3 cannot be simplified to 5x. Only terms with the same variable part combine.

**Solving before expanding.** Deal with the brackets first; the balance rule comes afterwards.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Expand 6(x + 4).

2. Expand −2(x − 7).

3. Solve 3(x + 1) = 18.

4. Solve 4(x − 2) = 20.

5. Solve 2(x + 3) + 3(x − 1) = 23.

6. Check your answer to question 5 in the original equation.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• The number outside a bracket multiplies every term inside.
• A minus outside the bracket flips the sign of every term inside.
• Expand first, collect like terms, then use the balance rule.
• Only like terms can be added together.
• Check the answer in the original equation.

objectives.text: Convert a fraction to a decimal by division.
Convert a terminating decimal to a fraction in lowest terms.

keyTerms.definition: The top number of a fraction: how many parts you have.
The bottom number: how many equal parts the whole was cut into.
A decimal that stops, such as 0.75.
A fraction where numerator and denominator share no common factor above 1.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
Fractions and decimals are two ways of writing the same quantity. Being able to move between them lets you compare numbers that are written differently.

By the end you will be able to:

• turn any fraction into a decimal
• turn a terminating decimal into a fraction in lowest terms
• compare a fraction with a decimal and say which is larger

sections.heading: Fraction to decimal
sections.body:
A fraction is a division waiting to happen. The line between the numbers means "divide". So to turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the top number by the bottom number.

The order matters: it is always top ÷ bottom. For 3/4 that is 3 ÷ 4, which is less than 1 — as it should be, since three quarters is less than a whole.

This is also how you compare a fraction with a decimal. Put both into the same form first, then compare.
sections.example:
3/4 means 3 divided by 4, which is 0.75. And 1/8 means 1 divided by 8, which is 0.125.

To compare 0.6 and 5/8: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, and 0.625 > 0.6, so 5/8 is larger.

sections.heading: Decimal to fraction
sections.body:
Read the decimal aloud and the fraction is usually in the words. 0.7 is "seven tenths", so it is 7/10. 0.35 is "thirty-five hundredths", so it is 35/100 — then cancel down to 7/20 by dividing top and bottom by 5.

The number of decimal places tells you the denominator: one place is tenths, two places is hundredths, three is thousandths. Then simplify.

An answer is in lowest terms when no number above 1 divides both top and bottom.
sections.example:
0.35 → 35/100.

    both divide by 5 → 7/20
    7 and 20 share no factor, so 7/20 is in lowest terms.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
Put these in order, smallest first: 0.6, 5/8, 0.58, 3/5.

Step 1 — convert every fraction to a decimal so they are all in one form.
    5/8 = 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625
    3/5 = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6

Step 2 — list them all as decimals.
    0.6, 0.625, 0.58, 0.6

Step 3 — compare place by place from the left. Writing them to the same number of places makes this easier:
    0.600, 0.625, 0.580, 0.600

Step 4 — order them.
    0.580 < 0.600 = 0.600 < 0.625

So: 0.58, then 0.6 and 3/5 (equal), then 5/8.

Notice that 3/5 and 0.6 are the same number written two ways.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body:
**Dividing bottom by top.** 3/4 is 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75, not 4 ÷ 3. The fraction is less than 1, so the decimal must be too.

**Comparing decimals by length.** 0.58 is not bigger than 0.6 because it has more digits. Line up the places: 0.580 against 0.600.

**Stopping before lowest terms.** 35/100 is correct but not finished. Cancel to 7/20.

**Forgetting the place value.** 0.35 is thirty-five hundredths, so 35/100 — not 35/10.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Write 1/4 as a decimal.

2. Write 2/5 as a decimal.

3. Write 0.8 as a fraction in lowest terms.

4. Write 0.45 as a fraction in lowest terms.

5. Which is larger, 0.7 or 3/4?

6. Put in order, smallest first: 1/2, 0.45, 3/5.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• A fraction line means divide: top ÷ bottom.
• Decimal places give the denominator: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
• Always cancel down to lowest terms.
• To compare, convert everything to one form first.
• Writing decimals to the same number of places makes comparing safe.

questions.question: What is the coefficient of x in the expression 7x + 4?
questions.explanation: The coefficient is the number multiplying the variable. In 7x, the 7 multiplies x, so the coefficient is 7. The 4 is a constant.

questions.question: Solve for x:  x + 9 = 16
questions.explanation: Nine has been added to x, so subtract 9 from both sides: x + 9 - 9 = 16 - 9, giving x = 7. Check: 7 + 9 = 16.

questions.question: Solve for x:  3x + 4 = 19
questions.explanation: Undo in reverse order. Subtract 4 from both sides: 3x = 15. Then divide both sides by 3: x = 5. Check: 3 x 5 + 4 = 19.

questions.question: Expand:  4(x + 3)
questions.explanation: The 4 multiplies every term inside the bracket, not just the first: 4 times x is 4x, and 4 times 3 is 12. So the answer is 4x + 12.

questions.question: Solve for x:  2(x - 5) = 14
questions.explanation: Expand first: 2x - 10 = 14. Add 10 to both sides: 2x = 24. Divide by 2: x = 12. Check: 2(12 - 5) = 2 x 7 = 14.

questions.question: A taxi charges 40 dollars to start plus 15 dollars per kilometre. Which expression gives the cost of a journey of k kilometres?
questions.explanation: The 40 is paid once, so it stands alone. The 15 is paid for each kilometre, so it multiplies k. That gives 40 + 15k.

questions.question: Solve for x:  5x - 3 = 2x + 12
questions.explanation: Collect the x terms on one side: subtract 2x from both sides to get 3x - 3 = 12. Add 3: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.

questions.question: Write 3/4 as a decimal.
questions.explanation: A fraction means divide. 3 divided by 4 is 0.75.

questions.question: Write 0.35 as a fraction in its lowest terms.
questions.explanation: 0.35 is thirty-five hundredths, so 35/100. Divide top and bottom by 5 to get 7/20.

questions.question: Which is larger: 0.6 or 5/8?
questions.explanation: Convert 5/8 to a decimal: 5 divided by 8 is 0.625. Since 0.625 is greater than 0.6, the fraction 5/8 is larger.
